bib.title: Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models

question: Which abilities of language models appear only above a certain scale, so that they cannot be predicted by extrapolating from smaller models?
contributions: Define emergent abilities of LLMs with respect to training FLOPs and parameters (Sec 2)
Survey emergent few-shot prompted tasks (Sec 3) and augmented prompting/finetuning strategies (Sec 4), collected in Table 1
Discuss explanations, routes beyond scaling, emergent risks and sociological shifts (Sec 5)
Appendix analyses: cross-entropy loss, alternative metrics, BIG-Bench task keywords, MMLU categories

results.claim: An ability is emergent if absent in smaller models and present in larger ones, so it cannot be predicted by extrapolating smaller-model scaling curves.
results.setup: Definition applied to pretrained Transformer LMs; scale measured as training FLOPs and parameters.
results.quote: An ability is emergent if it is not present in smaller models but is present in larger models.

results.claim: Chain-of-thought prompting beats standard prompting on GSM8K only at about 1e23 training FLOPs (~100B parameters).
results.setup: LaMDA, GSM8K, Fig 3A; results from Wei et al. 2022b.
results.quote: chain of thought prompting only surpasses standard prompting without intermediate steps when scaled to 1023 training FLOPs (∼100B parameters)
results.note: Table 1 lists 1.3E+23 FLOPs / 68B for the same item; text says ~100B.

results.claim: Instruction finetuning hurts models of 7e21 FLOPs (8B) or smaller and helps only near 1e23 FLOPs (~100B).
results.setup: LaMDA/FLAN, average over 10 NLU tasks, Fig 3B; Wei et al. 2022a.
results.quote: this instruction-ﬁnetuning technique hurts performance for models of 7·1021 training FLOPs (8B parameters) or smaller

results.claim: Scratchpad finetuning helps 8-digit addition only at about 9e19 FLOPs (40M parameters) or larger.
results.setup: LaMDA, 8-digit addition, Fig 3C; Nye et al. 2021.
results.quote: using a scratchpad only helps for models of ∼9 · 1019 training FLOPs (40M parameters) or larger

results.claim: On MMLU, GPT-3, Gopher and Chinchilla at ~1e22 FLOPs (~10B) or less are no better than guessing; 70B-280B at 3-5e23 FLOPs is substantially above random.
results.source: Hendrycks et al. 2021a; Rae et al. 2021; Hoffmann et al. 2022
results.quote: models of ∼1022 training FLOPs (∼10B parameters) or smaller do not perform better than guessing on average over all the topics

results.claim: Gopher performance on TruthfulQA jumps to more than 20% above random only at the largest model, 5e23 FLOPs (280B).
results.quote: performance jumps to more than 20% above random (Rae et al., 2021)

results.claim: Above-random one-shot Word in Context performance appeared only with PaLM at 2.5e24 FLOPs (540B), after GPT-3 and Chinchilla failed at ~5e23.
results.quote: above-random performance eventually emerged when PaLM was scaled to 2.5·1024 FLOPs (540B parameters)

results.claim: 3-digit addition/subtraction and 2-digit multiplication jump at 2e22 FLOPs (13B) for GPT-3 and 1e23 (68B) for LaMDA.
results.quote: sharply above random at 2 · 1022 training FLOPs (13B parameters) for GPT-3

results.claim: The True/False (P(True)) calibration technique beats standard calibration only at the largest scale, ~3e23 FLOPs (52B).
results.quote: the superiority of the True/False technique only emerges when scaled to the largest model scale of ∼3 · 1023 training FLOPs (52B parameters)
results.note: Table 1 prints 2.6E+23 for Calibration via P(True).

results.claim: 14 BIG-Bench tasks are near random for LaMDA 137B and GPT-3 175B but above random for PaLM 62B, so scale is not the only factor.
results.setup: Tasks listed in Appendix F; no ablation of PaLM differences.
results.quote: there are 14 BIG-Bench tasks5 for which LaMDA 137B and GPT-3 175B models perform at near-random, but PaLM 62B in fact achieves above-random performance

results.claim: Cross-entropy loss improves at scales where exact match, BLEU and accuracy are near random, for all six emergent BIG-Bench tasks (Outcome 2).
results.setup: Six few-shot BIG-Bench tasks, LaMDA; three generative, three classification; near random up to <=1e22 FLOPs / <=27B.
results.quote: We ﬁnd that all six BIG-Bench tasks fall under Outcome 2
results.note: Authors state this does not explain why downstream metrics are emergent nor predict the scale.

results.claim: Emergence on three generative BIG-Bench tasks appears under every BIG-Bench metric including BLEU, ROUGE and BLEURT, so exact match is not a full explanation.
results.setup: Modified arithmetic, IPA transliterate, periodic elements; Fig 7.
results.quote: the emergent behavior appears to be independent of which evaluation metric is used

results.claim: Of 210 BIG-Bench tasks, two co-authors hand-labelled emergence; no clear task-type trend, top keywords by percent emergent were analogical reasoning, word sense disambiguation, truthfulness, social reasoning, emotional understanding.
results.setup: Manual classification, subjective near-random threshold; 40 tasks unclassified.
results.quote: we manually classiﬁed all 210 BIG-Bench tasks as thus far emergent or not

results.claim: On MMLU, Social Science and Humanities show the largest jump from the second-largest to the largest model and STEM the smallest.
results.setup: Chinchilla 70B and Gopher 280B vs 7B models (around random, 25%), Figs 9-10.
results.quote: So the categories that improved the most from 7B to 70B/280B are humanities and social science, whereas STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics) improved the least.

results.claim: Smaller models can gain an ability later: a mixture-of-denoisers continued pretraining stage, T0 at 11B (encoder-decoder) and InstructGPT at 1.3B reach abilities earlier models needed far more scale for.
results.setup: Reported from Tay et al. 2022c, Sanh et al. 2022, Ouyang et al. 2022.
results.quote: enabled a 1.3B model to outperform much larger models in human-rater evaluations on a broad set of use cases

limits: A survey of prior results: apart from Appendix A/B re-analyses it runs no new experiments (Broader Impact: 'we surveyed results in the existing literature').
Authors state there are few compelling explanations for why abilities emerge and the cross-entropy analysis does not predict the scale of emergence.
Emergence scale depends on data quality, training and model family; it is not an immutable property of the ability (Sec 2, 5.2).
Scale proxies (FLOPs, parameters, WikiText103 perplexity) are correlated; the correlation may not hold for retrieval or MoE models (Sec 2, 5.3).
BIG-Bench emergence labels are manual and depend on a subjective definition of near-random (App A.3); Logical arguments has only 32 samples (Fig 6).
Thresholds come from few model sizes per family (e.g. three PaLM sizes), so curves are coarse.
Dated: later work (Schaeffer et al. 2023) argues metric choice explains apparent emergence; not in this paper.
practices: Judge whether a technique helps at your model scale: a technique counts as emergent if it shows no improvement or is harmful versus baseline until large enough scale (Sec 4).
Do not read emergence thresholds as properties of the ability: they are tied to model family, data and training (Sec 2, 5.2).
Check the evaluation metric: exact match on long targets can disguise incremental gains, though emergence persisted under partial-credit metrics and classification (Sec 5.1, App A.2).
Treat emergence as a function of many correlated variables rather than a single scale axis (Sec 5.3).

terms.definition: Emergence is when quantitative changes in a system result in qualitative changes in behavior.
An ability is emergent if it is not present in smaller models but is present in larger models.
includes a few input-output examples in the model's context (input) as a preamble before asking the model to perform the task for an unseen inference-time example
a dramatic change in overall behavior that would not have been foreseen by examining smaller-scale systems
